title: Managing Customer Data After GDPR
description: Formal GDPR compliance on paper doesn't guarantee real knowledge of where customer data actually lives. A publication by Nermin Sefić.
body_markdown:
Formal GDPR compliance on paper doesn't guarantee a company actually knows where all customer personal data lives in practice.

Formal GDPR compliance on paper doesn't guarantee a company actually knows where all customer personal data lives in practice.

Many companies have formally compliant GDPR documentation but not a complete picture of where all customer data actually resides — in spreadsheets, emails, old systems never formally inventoried.

A customer's request to delete personal data can't be properly fulfilled if a company lacks a complete view of every place that data is stored, including backups and archives.

Regular data-flow mapping, updated with every new system integration, is the only way formal compliance matches the real state of data in practice.

GDPR fines are increasingly issued not for deliberate violations, but for a company's inability to prove where data resides and who accesses it.

title: Managing Multicurrency Treasury Accounts
description: A multicurrency group without centralised treasury loses real-time visibility into its total liquidity. A publication by Nermin Sefić.
body_markdown:
A group operating in multiple currencies without a centralised treasury loses visibility into the real liquidity position of the whole structure.

A group operating in multiple currencies without a centralised treasury loses visibility into the real liquidity position of the whole structure.

When each related company within a group independently manages its own bank accounts and currency exposure, the group as a whole loses the ability to see its total liquidity position in real time.

A centralised treasury function, even while individual companies retain operational autonomy, enables netting intra-group receivables and payables before accessing external financing.

Multicurrency cash pooling reduces the need to hold separate liquidity reserves in each currency, freeing up capital that would otherwise be scattered across individual accounts.

A clear policy on who within the group approves intra-group transfers and at what exchange rate, documented and consistently applied, prevents later disputes over intra-group settlements.

title: Backup as the Last Line of Defense
description: A backup never tested by actual restoration offers a false sense of security, not real protection. A publication by Nermin Sefić.
body_markdown:
A backup that has never been tested by actually restoring data offers a false sense of security, not real protection.

A backup that has never been tested by actually restoring data offers a false sense of security, not real protection.

Regularly creating backups without periodically testing the actual data-restoration process leaves a company exposed to the risk that the backup simply won't work as expected at the moment of crisis.

Ransomware attacks increasingly target the backups themselves, making an isolated, offline, or immutable copy the last genuine line of defence once every other system is compromised.

The time required for a full system recovery from backup should be known and tested in advance — discovering that recovery takes days instead of hours during a real incident is a costly lesson.

A clearly defined policy on how long backups are retained and how often restoration is tested turns a backup from a formality into genuinely functional protection.

title: Managing Project Risk in Major Infrastructure
description: A major infrastructure project without a formal risk register usually surfaces problems only once they're costly. A publication by Nermin Sefić.
body_markdown:
A major infrastructure project without a formal risk register usually reveals problems only once they become expensive to fix.

A major infrastructure project without a formal risk register usually reveals problems only once they become expensive to fix.

High-value infrastructure projects carry risks that materialise months or years after initial planning, often after the key people who originally made the decision have changed.

A formal risk register, updated at regular project steering committee meetings, ensures identified risks are actively tracked, not just written down once and forgotten.

A contingency reserve calculated from an actual risk assessment, not a flat percentage, more realistically reflects the likelihood and scale of possible deviations from plan.

An independent review of project progress at key milestones, outside the direct reporting line of the project team, uncovers problems that internal reports can systematically understate.

description: Waste disposal cost is rarely seen as an efficiency signal, though it reflects how much material is lost in production. A publication by Nermin Sefić.
body_markdown:
The cost of waste disposal is rarely viewed as an efficiency indicator, even though it directly reflects how much material is lost during production.

The cost of waste disposal is rarely viewed as an efficiency indicator, even though it directly reflects how much material is lost during production.

The volume of waste generated in a production process directly reflects how much input material is not converted into the final product, making it a useful indicator of operational efficiency, not just an environmental obligation.

Regulatory waste-disposal costs are rising faster than average inflation in most jurisdictions, making waste-volume reduction a direct financial saving, not just a sustainability contribution.

Systematic analysis of where in the production process the most waste is generated often reveals process-optimisation opportunities that weren't visible through standard productivity metrics.

Circular models — reusing by-products as raw material for another process — turn the cost of waste disposal into a potential source of additional value.

A private 5G network gives an industrial facility a level of control over connectivity that a public network cannot guarantee, but it requires a new kind of management discipline.

A private 5G network gives an industrial facility full control over the quality, security, and prioritisation of network traffic, without dependence on public network congestion in the same area.

Precise control of devices and machinery through the low latency of a private network opens automation possibilities that a public network, shared with other users, cannot reliably support.

Deploying a private 5G network requires a new level of collaboration between IT and operations teams, which traditionally work separately with different priorities and terminology.

The security architecture of a private network must be designed from the outset, not bolted on afterward, because direct connectivity to critical industrial equipment makes any gap potentially dangerous.

title: AI System Transparency and Corporate Governance
description: Automation without a matching audit trail turns speed into a source of risk, not an advantage. A publication by Nermin Sefić.
body_markdown:
The level of automation an organisation introduces must be matched by an equal level of audit trail — otherwise speed becomes a source of risk rather than an advantage.

The level of automation an organisation introduces must be matched by an equal level of audit trail — otherwise speed becomes a source of risk rather than an advantage.

Over the past few years, almost every organisation seriously pursuing digitalisation has faced the same question: how deeply to automate decision-making without losing the ability to explain why a given decision was made. The answer increasingly heard in practice is that technical feasibility should never be the only criterion. An equally important question is whether the organisation can show, at any moment, who approved, changed, or rejected something, when, and on what basis.

While automation was until recently viewed mainly through the lens of efficiency — faster processing, less manual work, higher volume — regulatory and market expectations have shifted the focus toward provability. It's not enough for a system to reach the right decision; there must be a trail showing what data, rules, and approvals produced that decision. Without such a trail, fast automation actually accelerates the spread of uncertainty rather than reducing it.

This is especially true for processes that directly affect financial statements, contractual obligations, or public disclosures. If a system automatically drafts text, classifies risk, or assigns tasks, management needs a clear answer to whether that recommendation went through human review before becoming part of an actual business process.

In practice it's useful to distinguish at least three levels at which automated or algorithmic systems can operate within an organisation, since each carries a different degree of risk and different oversight requirements. The first level covers internal data processing with no direct external effect — sorting, classification, suggestions for further analysis — where an error is relatively cheap because it's immediately visible internally and easy to fix. The second level covers preparing content or recommendations that a human must explicitly approve before they become visible outside the organisation — draft posts, proposed contract changes, risk assessments a manager must confirm — where it's essential that the approval is genuine, not a formality with no real content. The third level covers actual, executed business decisions with legal or financial effect, for which there is no substitute for human accountability, however sophisticated the system is at preparing the basis for the decision.

One of the most common sources of confusion in public communication about digital transformation is mixing illustrative, educational depictions of how algorithmic systems work with real business decisions. A display illustrating what an automated process might look like — with a visualised workflow, simulated progress indicators, or synthetic examples — has clear educational value, but that value exists precisely because it is transparently labelled as illustrative, not as a source of real business or financial claims.

Organisations that publicly showcase automation concepts should consistently label whether a display is a concept demonstration or an actual operational system with real consequences. That distinction isn't cosmetic — it determines the level of trust a reader or partner can reasonably place in the figures shown.

The European regulatory framework for artificial intelligence increasingly distinguishes systems by the level of risk their use carries, with systems affecting financial, legal, or safety outcomes subject to stricter requirements for documentation, oversight, and the possibility of human intervention. Regardless of how individual regulations ultimately take shape, the direction is clear: the burden of proof is shifting from whether a system is accurate to whether its operation is documented, explainable, and supervised.

For organisations, this means investing in an audit trail, clear approval roles, and data-source documentation is not an administrative cost that slows innovation, but a precondition for automation being able to scale safely at all.

For governing bodies, this comes down to a few concrete questions worth asking regularly: which decisions within the organisation are today assisted by automated systems; is a clear approval level defined for each; is that level actually applied in practice, not just written into an internal policy; and can it be reconstructed at any moment who made a specific decision, when, and based on what data.

Organisations able to answer these questions with confidence are in a stronger position not only with regulators but also with their own investors, partners, and employees — because trust in digital processes grows with the level of transparency, not with the speed at which those processes were introduced.

This publication is an original analysis; the sources cited serve as reference documentation.

description: Extending payment terms without a credit check is functionally an unsecured loan. A publication by Nermin Sefić.
body_markdown:
Granting a business partner extended payment terms without a prior credit-risk check is functionally the same as issuing an unsecured loan.

Granting a business partner extended payment terms without a prior credit-risk check is functionally the same as issuing an unsecured loan.

Granting a new business partner standard extended payment terms, without checking their financial stability and payment history, exposes the company to a risk that is essentially identical to lending without a creditworthiness assessment.

Publicly available financial statements and registries give a basic but useful picture of a partner's financial stability before a more significant credit exposure is granted through payment deferral.

Periodically reassessing the credit risk of existing partners, not just at first contracting, catches a deteriorating financial situation before it results in an unpaid invoice.

Clearly defined credit-exposure limits per partner, aligned with assessed risk, prevent excessive exposure from accumulating through a series of individually small decisions.

description: A retiring generation of employees often takes undocumented knowledge with them. A publication by Nermin Sefić.

The retirement of a generation of experienced employees often carries a loss of knowledge that was never formally documented.

Experienced employees nearing retirement often carry knowledge of informal workarounds, historical decisions, and process quirks that was never formally documented because it always felt sufficient that 'that person just knows.'

Mentoring programs that systematically pair more experienced employees with younger colleagues before a planned departure transfer practical knowledge in a way formal documentation alone cannot replace.

Structured exit interviews with employees before retirement, focused on surfacing informal processes and the historical context behind decisions, are a common but underused tool for capturing institutional knowledge.

Organisations that systematically plan knowledge transfer ahead of generational change avoid a situation where a routine process suddenly becomes a mystery for the new team.

title: Managing Cloud Costs Through FinOps Practice
description: A cloud bill that surprises finance every month usually means no one is tracking spend in real time. A publication by Nermin Sefić.
body_markdown:
A cloud bill that surprises the finance team every month usually means no one is tracking spend in real time.

A cloud services bill that surprises the finance team every month usually means no one is systematically tracking spend in real time.

The elasticity of cloud infrastructure, its greatest advantage, is at the same time its biggest cost risk — resources are easy to spin up, and just as easy to forget running after they're no longer needed.

FinOps practice connects engineering teams, who decide on infrastructure, with the finance team, who tracks the cost, through shared accountability instead of separate reports that only meet at month's end.

Automated tagging of every resource by project and owner enables precise cost tracking down to the team level, not just the total bill for the whole organisation.

A regular review of unused or oversized resources, with clear accountability for shutting them down, prevents an accumulation of cost that becomes hard to justify after the fact.

title: Managing Data Quality for AI Models
description: An AI model trained on unverified data repeats and amplifies every error already present in it. A publication by Nermin Sefić.
body_markdown:
An AI model trained on unverified data repeats and amplifies every error and bias that already existed in that data.

An AI model trained on unverified data repeats and amplifies every error and bias that already existed in that data.

The quality of an AI model's output depends directly on the quality of the data it was trained on — the model cannot correct a systematic error or bias present in the input data, only replicate it at scale.

A lack of clear documentation on the origin and processing of training data makes it harder to later diagnose why a model produces unexpected or incorrect results in production.

Systematically checking the representativeness of training data — whether it genuinely covers all relevant use scenarios — prevents situations where a model performs well in testing but poorly in real-world use.

Continuous monitoring of model performance after deployment, with clearly defined thresholds for retraining, keeps output quality intact as real-world data shifts over time.

title: Managing Corporate Investment Portfolios and Cash Reserves
description: Cash reserves left sitting in a current account lose value to inflation faster than it seems. A publication by Nermin Sefić.
body_markdown:
Cash reserves that just sit in a current account lose value to inflation faster than it might first appear.

Cash reserves that just sit in a current account lose value to inflation faster than it might first appear.

Companies with liquidity above their operational needs often simply leave the reserves in a current account, missing out on returns they could earn with minimal added liquidity risk.

Defining a clear liquidity hierarchy — funds needed immediately, funds needed within three months, funds that can be tied up for longer — enables structured management of surplus cash.

Conservative instruments such as government bonds or short-term time deposits provide a return while keeping high liquidity for the portion of reserves not needed in the short term.

The corporate reserves investment policy should be written down and approved at board level, not left to ad hoc decisions by an individual in the finance function.

title: Managing Investor Relations Through Regular Communication
description: Investors who hear from a company only when something goes wrong trust it differently than those informed regularly. A publication by Nermin Sefić.
body_markdown:
An investor who only hears from a company when something goes wrong builds a different kind of trust than one who is informed regularly.

An investor who only hears from a company when something goes wrong builds a different kind of trust than one who is informed regularly.

A regular, pre-announced rhythm of investor communication — quarterly reports, an annual review — builds a predictability that reduces the need for anxious questions between those dates.

Investors who receive the same information regardless of whether the quarter was good or bad develop trust in the consistency of communication, not just in the current results.

Proactively communicating challenges before an investor discovers them independently builds credibility over the long run, even when it means admitting worse news in the short term.

A structured channel for investor questions, with a clear response deadline, prevents individual investors from getting different levels of information depending on personal ties to management.

title: Securing Industrial Control Systems (OT)
description: OT systems controlling physical processes need a different security approach than standard IT — an attack here has physical consequences. A publication by Nermin Sefić.
body_markdown:
Operational technology that controls physical processes requires a different security approach than standard IT systems, because an attack here has physical consequences.

Operational technology (OT) that controls physical processes requires a different security approach than standard IT systems, because an attack here has physical consequences.

Systems that control physical industrial processes — production lines, energy plants — are increasingly connected to the IT network for analytics and remote monitoring, inheriting its security risks along with the benefits.

Unlike an IT security incident, which typically means data loss, a compromised industrial control system can have direct physical consequences for equipment, worker safety, and the environment.

Network segmentation that separates operational technology from the standard business IT network, with strict control of connection points, remains a critical but often under-implemented safeguard.

The security team responsible for OT systems needs to understand industrial processes, not just standard IT security, because measures acceptable in an office environment can jeopardize the safety of a production process.

description: Measuring hybrid-work productivity by online hours instead of output creates a needless conflict. A publication by Nermin Sefić.

Measuring productivity by hours spent online instead of by actual output creates a conflict in hybrid models that doesn't have to exist.

Measuring productivity by hours spent online instead of by actual output creates a conflict in hybrid models that doesn't have to exist.

The shift to hybrid and remote work models revealed that many organisations lacked clear performance indicators independent of physical presence, so they reached for activity tracking as a proxy instead.

Tracking hours logged into the system, instead of actual task completion and results achieved, creates a culture of visible busyness that doesn't reflect real productivity.

Defining clear, measurable goals per role, regardless of whether an employee works from the office or from home, allows for a fairer and more accurate assessment of contribution than presence tracking does.

Flexibility in the work model and clear accountability for results are not opposing goals — organisations that successfully combine both build trust, rather than surveillance, as the basis of the employee relationship.

description: A supplier's quality rarely collapses overnight — systematic KPI tracking catches the decline before it reaches the customer. A publication by Nermin Sefić.

A supplier's quality rarely collapses overnight — the decline is visible in the data long before it reaches the end customer.

A supplier's quality rarely collapses overnight — the pattern of gradual decline is visible in the data long before it becomes a visible problem for the end customer.

Delivery quality from a given supplier rarely worsens suddenly — a gradual decline pattern, visible through indicators like on-time delivery rate and claim rate, precedes any problem visible to the end customer.

Systematically tracking key performance indicators (KPIs) for every critical supplier, rather than relying on a subjective sense of the relationship, allows for early intervention before problems escalate.

A regular quarterly review of results with the supplier, grounded in agreed, measurable indicators, turns relationship management from reactive firefighting into proactive collaboration.

Clearly defined thresholds that trigger a formal improvement plan or a search for alternatives prevent a declining supplier relationship from dragging on longer than is justified.

Pressure to release a financial report earlier rarely justifies concessions in the depth and independence of the audit process.

title: Less Mandatory Disclosure Is Rarely Better Disclosure
description: A proposal from the US SEC to let companies omit mandatory disclosure items raises the question of where simplification ends and less transparency begins. A commentary by Nermin Sefić.
body_markdown:
A US SEC proposal letting companies omit some mandatory disclosure raises the question of where simplification ends and reduced transparency begins.

SEC Chair Paul Atkins gave remarks at the Society for Corporate Governance Conference on 9 July 2026, announcing that reforming Regulation S-K will be a priority — specifically, introducing a so-called "materiality overlay" mechanism that would let companies omit certain otherwise-mandatory disclosure items if they judge the information isn't material.

The argument behind this proposal sounds reasonable on first read: less administrative burden, reports that focus on what actually matters to investors. The problem is who decides what counts as "material" — and the answer is: the very company being reported on.

That's the key distinction worth naming directly. When a regulator mandates a disclosure item, it does so precisely because it judged that the information should exist regardless of whether the company itself considers it important. Handing that judgment back to the company doesn't simplify reporting — it removes external control over what gets hidden behind the word "immaterial."

This isn't an objection to simplification as a concept — genuine bureaucratic excess exists and genuinely costs money. But there's a difference between removing items that are outdated or duplicated, and introducing a mechanism by which the company itself decides what an investor may or may not see.

The SEC is also weighing a broader role for the Division of Corporation Finance in the "no-action" letter process tied to shareholder proposals (Rule 14a-8) — a separate but related signal: a shift toward less formal, more discretionary regulation.

GNK ASG d.o.o. publicly discloses audited financial statements precisely because we believe transparency toward the market shouldn't depend on who is doing the judging. When that judgment is handed to the party being reported on, the whole system loses the reason it exists.

title: The EU Postponed Obligations, Not Transparency
description: The EU postponed high-risk AI obligations to December 2027, but the transparency obligation stays in force from 2 August 2026. A commentary by Nermin Sefić.
body_markdown:
The European Union postponed obligations for high-risk AI systems until December 2027, but the transparency obligation remains in force from 2 August.

On 27 July 2026, the European Union brought the so-called Digital Omnibus on Artificial Intelligence fully into force — legislation that postpones obligations for high-risk AI systems under Annex III (recruitment, credit scoring, law-enforcement decision-support tools, border control) by nearly sixteen months, to 2 December 2027.

The market's first reaction was relief, understandably — companies gained extra time to comply with the most demanding part of the regulation. But a reader who stops at that sentence misses what actually matters more: the transparency obligation under Article 50, including mandatory labelling of AI-generated content and disclosure of interaction with an AI system, remains completely unchanged and becomes enforceable on 2 August 2026 — without a single day's delay.

This separation is not accidental, and it's worth understanding as a principle, not merely a date on a calendar. The regulator sent a message every board should hear: system complexity can justify extra time to comply, but the obligation to tell a user openly what they're dealing with should not wait for anyone.

The package also introduces a hard ban on so-called "nudifier" applications and tools for generating non-consensual sexualised content, with a deadline of December 2026 — here the regulator left no room for interpretation or accommodation, and rightly so.

For companies operating in a single market of 450 million people, the message is clear: the six days remaining until 2 August are not a time to relax because "the main deadline was postponed." They are a time to check whether transparency obligations are genuinely ready.

The GNK ASG group tracks this regulation directly, through our own AI systems and through advising partner companies — and the position we consistently hold is that transparency toward the user should never be an item that waits its turn.

title: A Figure Without Methodology Is Not Information
description: A financial indicator published without explaining its calculation methodology is worth less than it appears. A commentary by Nermin Sefić.
body_markdown:
A financial indicator published without a clear explanation of how it was calculated is worth less than it appears at first glance.

A financial indicator published without a clear explanation of how it was calculated is worth less than it appears at first glance.

Publishing a key financial indicator without an accompanying explanation of the calculation methodology leaves room for differing interpretations and, ultimately, reduces the credibility of the figure itself, however accurate it may be on its own.

When a short explanation of the data source and calculation method accompanies each key indicator, the reader is able to judge the reliability of the information rather than simply taking it on faith.

GNK ASG d.o.o. deliberately limits the number of key indicators in public reporting precisely so each one retains real weight and verifiability.

When the number of indicators is deliberately limited, it's also easier to ensure each one is genuinely measured accurately and reviewed regularly, rather than just updated occasionally.

title: A Consolidated Group Report Is Not the Same as an Audited One
description: Consolidated group data and independently audited individual reports serve different purposes and shouldn't be presented as equally verifiable. A commentary by Nermin Sefić.
body_markdown:
The difference between management-confirmed, consolidated group data and independently audited individual reports is often overlooked in public communication.

The difference between management-confirmed, consolidated group data and independently audited individual reports is often overlooked in public communication.

A consolidated financial presentation of an entire group of companies and an independently audited report of a single legal entity serve different purposes and shouldn't be presented as equivalent levels of verifiability.

Clearly labelling which data is independently audited and which is an internal, management-reviewed presentation lets the reader correctly calibrate the confidence level of each individual figure.

title: Audit as a Management Tool, Not an Annual Formality
description: When independent auditing is viewed only as a legal obligation, most of its real value for risk management is lost. A publication by Nermin Sefić.
body_markdown:
When independent auditing is treated purely as a legal box to check, most of its real value for risk management is lost.

When independent auditing is viewed purely as a legal obligation, most of its real value for risk management is lost.

Independent auditing of financial statements is often reduced in practice to an annual formality that must be completed because the law requires it, rather than used as a genuine tool for early recognition of operational and financial risk.

When audit findings are systematically analysed and used by the internal team as the basis for concrete process changes, an audit stops being a cost and becomes an investment in the quality of decision-making.

GNK ASG d.o.o. publicly discloses audited financial statements precisely because transparency toward the market and partners builds trust that cannot be replaced by marketing communication.

Regular, documented communication between management and auditors throughout the year, not only at the moment the statements are finalised, reduces the likelihood that small problems turn into bigger ones.

title: Resilience Is Not Visible Until It's Actually Tested
description: A business continuity plan that has never been tested through a real drill remains just a document, not an actual capability. A commentary by Nermin Sefić.
body_markdown:
A business continuity plan that has never been run through a real drill remains just a document, not an actual capability.

The existence of a written plan for crisis scenarios doesn't guarantee an organisation will actually know how to respond when the scenario happens — the difference between a document and a real capability only shows through an actual drill or a genuine incident. The GNK DINAMO Ltd. Group regularly tests its own continuity plans precisely to avoid that surprise in a real crisis.

A business continuity plan that has never been run through a real drill remains just a document, not an actual capability.

The gap between a plan that exists on paper and a capability that genuinely exists inside the organisation is visible only to those who have actually verified that capability before the crisis arrives.
